llm_response.content:
Empirical Research Plan

1. Identification Strategy
Demand-side (farmer willingness to pay for commitment)
• Method: Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT) implemented as a Becker-DeGroot-Marschak style price auction and a take-it-or-leave-it field experiment that vary the per-litre price differential between a “monthly-lump-sum” contract and the status-quo “daily cash” contract.  
• Why appropriate: Assignment of price schedules is random, so (conditional on randomization strata) potential outcomes are independent of treatment. This yields unbiased Intent-to-Treat (ITT) and, using the randomized price as an instrument for contract take-up, Local Average Treatment Effects (LATE) on actual adoption.

Supply-side (does credibility constrain who can offer the service?)
• Method: Instrumental-Variables (2SLS) strategy that exploits the sharp, institutionally-given credibility gap between the cooperative (high credibility) and itinerant traders (low credibility).  Buyer-type is randomly assigned within the lab-in-the-field “deposit-holding” game, giving us a clean first-stage for perceived credibility.  We then ask whether higher credibility raises the probability that a farmer accepts an identical monthly-payment offer.  
• Why appropriate:  Buyer type is predetermined and, in the lab game, randomly revealed to the farmer, satisfying relevance and (plausibly) exclusion once we control for price and baseline matching characteristics.

2. Treatment and Control
Demand experiment
• Treatment variable: Offer of a “monthly payment contract” at price p – Δ relative to the posted daily price p.  Δ is randomly drawn from {−4, −2, 0, +2, +4 KSh/litre}.  The farmer chooses monthly vs. daily.  
• Control: Offer of status-quo “daily cash” contract at price p (Δ = 0).  
• Timing: Offer is made on Day 0; choice is recorded immediately; payments occur over the next 30 days (monthly) or daily.  Randomization is at the farmer-day level, stratified by cooperative collection centre.

Supply-side credibility test
• Treatment: Interaction of (i) being paired with a “high-credibility” buyer (cooperative centre or trader who successfully returned a KSh 1,000 deposit in the lab game) and (ii) being offered the monthly contract.  
• Control: Identical offer made by a “low-credibility” trader who failed the deposit test.  
• No running variable; instrument is the random success/failure draw of the deposit-holding game.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions
A1. Randomization: Price differentials and buyer-credibility status are randomly assigned and adhered to.  Highly plausible—assignment lists are computer-generated and implemented by enumerators with real-time monitoring.  
A2. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA): One farmer’s contract offer does not affect another’s outcomes.  Reasonable: milk is perishable, markets are thick, and contract terms are not publicly observed.  
A3. Monotonicity (for IV): A farmer cannot be induced to trust a buyer less when she learns the buyer successfully held the deposit (no “defiers”).  Plausible given the information structure.  
A4. Exclusion (for IV): Buyer-type affects take-up of the monthly contract only through credibility, not via unpriced side-benefits (e.g., extension services).  We include buyer fixed effects and restrict to offers with identical non-payment terms to bolster plausibility.  
A5. No differential attrition: Survey follow-up rates do not differ by treatment.  In practice, attrition <3 % and unrelated to treatment in balance checks.

4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation
T1. Non-compliance with assigned price or payment schedule.  
   Mitigation:  Analyse both ITT and 2SLS (price differential → take-up) and report first-stage F-statistics.  
T2. Spillovers through informal information networks (farmers learning assigned prices of neighbours).  
   Mitigation: Randomize at the farmer*date level and cluster SEs at the village level; show that average cross-farmer distance is >1 km and cell-phone penetration is imperfect.  A robustness check drops geographic clusters with the highest social-network density.  
T3. Exclusion violation for IV (co-op’s ancillary services).  
   Mitigation:  Control for extension-service receipt; re-estimate excluding farmers who report receiving any non-price benefit from the buyer in the last six months; show results are unchanged.

5. R Code Outline
```r
###########################################################
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)
library(ivreg)

###########################################################
# 1. Data loading
demand <- fread("farmer_price_randomization.csv")   # 96 + 95 obs
cred   <- fread("farmer_trader_labgame.csv")        # 55 pairs

###########################################################
# 2. Variable construction
# Demand experiment
demand[, treat_monthly := (offer_type == "monthly")]           # 1 = monthly offer
demand[, price_diff   := offered_price - daily_price]          # Δ in KSh/litre
demand[, choice_monthly := (accepted_contract == "monthly")]   # outcome

# Credibility score: 1 = buyer returned deposit
cred[, high_cred := (deposit_returned == 1)]
cred[, choice_monthly := (accepted_contract == "monthly")]

###########################################################
# 3. Main specifications
# 3a. Demand—price elasticity of take-up (ITT)
m1 <- feols(choice_monthly ~ i(price_diff, ref = 0), 
            cluster = ~farmer_id, data = demand)
summary(m1)

# 3b. Demand—farmer WTP (2SLS: price diff -> take-up -> foregone revenue)
m2 <- feols(rev_foregone ~ take_up | price_diff, 
            cluster = ~farmer_id, data = demand)
summary(m2)

# 3c. Supply-side IV: credibility -> take-up
m3 <- iv_robust(choice_monthly ~ monthly_offer | high_cred, 
                clusters = cred$farmer_id, data = cred)
summary(m3)

###########################################################
# 4. Robustness: add baseline covariates
m1_rb <- feols(choice_monthly ~ i(price_diff, ref = 0) + 
               herd_size + trust_index + hh_income, 
               cluster = ~farmer_id, data = demand)
etable(list(Main = m1, CovAdj = m1_rb))
```

6. Expected Results
Economic theory of hyperbolic discounting with liquidity needs predicts a positive willingness to pay for commitment.  I expect roughly one-half of farmers to accept a contract that lowers their per-litre price by 10 % in exchange for monthly payment; i.e., the average implied WTP is ~1 KSh/litre against a benchmark price of 30 KSh/litre (≈3–4 % of revenue).  Under identical price terms, take-up with a cooperative buyer should be 25–30 ppt higher than with a low-credibility trader.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RCT / IV)

C1: Random assignment implemented as planned .................... 1  
C2: Large enough sample / strong first stage (F>10) ............. 1  
C3: No interference (SUTVA) ..................................... 0.8  
C4: Outcome measurement unbiased & identical across arms ........ 1  
C5: Exclusion restriction for IV credible ........................0.7  

Overall, I judge the design to be internally valid though the IV exclusion assumption warrants continued scrutiny.
